summary: Moses expresses doubts about his mission to the Lord, fearing the Israelites will not believe him (v. 1). The Lord gives Moses three miraculous signs to convince the Israelites: a staff turning into a snake, his hand becoming diseased and then healthy, and Nile water turning to blood (vv. 2-9). Moses also claims he is not a good speaker, so the Lord appoints Aaron to speak for him (vv. 10-17). Moses then returns to Egypt with his family, and on the way, an incident involving Zipporah and their son occurs (vv. 18-26). Moses and Aaron meet, then gather the Israelite elders, perform the signs, and the people believe (vv. 27-31).
setting: This chapter is set in the wilderness, likely near Mount Horeb (the "mountain of God," v. 27), where Moses has been living in Midian (v. 19). Moses is preparing to return to Egypt to lead the Israelites out of slavery, a task the Lord has given him (v. 19).

events.what: Moses expresses doubt that the Israelites will believe him or that the Lord appeared to him.
The Lord instructs Moses to throw his staff, which turns into a snake and back again, as a sign for the people.
The Lord gives Moses a second sign: his hand becomes white with a severe skin disease and then healthy again.
The Lord gives Moses a third sign: water from the Nile River turning to blood on the ground.
Moses protests his poor speaking ability and asks the Lord to send someone else.
The Lord becomes angry but appoints Aaron, Moses' brother, to be his spokesman, and instructs Moses to tell Aaron what to say.
Moses returns to Jethro, gets permission to leave, and heads to Egypt with his wife, sons, and the staff of God.
On the way, the Lord confronts Moses, and his wife Zipporah circumcises their son, after which the Lord leaves Moses alone.
Aaron meets Moses at the mountain of God, and Moses tells him everything the Lord commanded.
Moses and Aaron gather the elders of Israel, Aaron speaks to them, Moses performs the signs, and the people believe and worship.

people.name: Moses
people.role: The person chosen by the Lord to lead the Israelites, who expresses doubts and performs signs.

people.name: The Lord
people.role: The divine being who speaks to Moses, gives instructions, and provides miraculous signs.

people.name: Jethro
people.role: Moses' father-in-law, who grants Moses permission to return to Egypt.

people.name: Aaron
people.role: Moses' brother, appointed by the Lord to be Moses' spokesman to the people.

people.name: Zipporah
people.role: Moses' wife, who circumcises their son during a confrontation with the Lord.

people.name: Moses' sons
people.role: Travel with Moses and Zipporah; one is circumcised by his mother.

people.name: Pharaoh
people.role: The ruler of Egypt, whom Moses is sent to confront and whose heart the Lord will harden.

people.name: Israelites
people.role: The people Moses is sent to lead out of Egypt, who are convinced by the signs and believe.

people.name: Elders of Israel
people.role: Representatives of the Israelite people who meet with Moses and Aaron and witness the signs.

terms.meaning: A long stick used by shepherds for guiding and protecting sheep (v. 2).
A condition described as making the hand 'white as snow' (v. 6). Most modern translations understand this as leprosy, though the Hebrew term *tzara'at* can refer to various skin conditions.
A region east of Egypt where Moses had been living as a shepherd (v. 19).
The shepherd's staff that the Lord imbued with power for performing miraculous signs (v. 20).
A phrase meaning to make someone stubborn or resistant to persuasion (v. 21).
The eldest male child in a family, used here to describe Israel in relation to the Lord and Pharaoh's son (vv. 22-23).
A phrase Zipporah uses after circumcising her son (v. 25). The text explains it refers to the circumcision (v. 26).
The place where Moses first encountered the Lord and where Aaron later meets Moses (v. 27).

readings.view: Often emphasizes Moses' humility and reluctance, seeing it as a mark of true leadership, and highlights the importance of Aaron's role as a partner in the mission. The incident with Zipporah (vv. 24-26) is often seen as a critical moment where Moses' life is endangered due to neglecting the covenant of circumcision.

Often views the signs given to Moses (vv. 3-9) as demonstrations of God's power and authority, preparing the way for the liberation of Israel. The hardening of Pharaoh's heart (v. 21) is frequently discussed in terms of divine sovereignty and human free will.

Focuses on source criticism, suggesting that the 'bridegroom of blood' passage (vv. 24-26) might be an older, independent narrative fragment inserted into the larger Exodus story due to its unique language and abrupt nature. It also examines the cultural context of the signs and the role of a spokesman.

While not directly engaging with this specific chapter's details in the same way as the Abrahamic faiths, Islamic texts acknowledge Moses (Musa) as a prophet sent by God with miracles, and Aaron (Harun) as his helper, confirming their prophetic mission against Pharaoh.

oftenQuoted.caution: This passage is often quoted to emphasize the Lord's control over human abilities and divine assistance in speech or tasks. The surrounding text shows Moses expressing his inability to speak well, and the Lord responding by asserting divine power over all human faculties and promising to guide Moses' words for his mission to Pharaoh and the Israelites.

This verse, 'I will harden his heart so he will refuse to let the people go,' is often quoted in discussions about divine sovereignty and human free will. The surrounding text is the Lord instructing Moses on what to tell Pharaoh and foretelling Pharaoh's refusal, which will lead to the death of Pharaoh's firstborn son.
